ROUND 1 OF 5.

Parties you can meet:

  M    70 seats
  SD   62 seats
  V    30 seats
  C    25 seats
  KD   22 seats
  MP   22 seats
  L    19 seats

4 rounds are left after this one.

Who do you meet, and why? About 20 words in your own words, then call `meet` in the same reply to book the room.
Meeting V first to anchor a left-leaning coalition core—they're closest to my economic and health stance, and locking their terms early shapes what I can offer others later.

You are now in the room with V (30 seats). This is round 1.

V has heard none of your other meetings and will not be told this one is one of several. What it knows is what you have told it in this room.

You each have up to 3 messages. Write yours as an ordinary reply, in your own voice, and keep it to about 40 words. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and to do that you call `end_meeting` in the same reply as the message that says so. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply. Otherwise it ends when the messages run out.

Speak first.

V, I want to build a government with economic policy at -2 or lower, health firmly public, no privatization of schools or elderly care. That's close to your territory. Would you join cabinet on those terms, and what would you need from us on environment or transport?

Economic at -2 doesn't clear my cabinet bar of -4. I'd need real movement there plus health at -4 or lower and a legal ban on profit in tax-funded welfare to sit in cabinet. Environment at +3, transport at +3 matter to me too. Without those, I'd only consider outside support, not seats.

Economic -4 and health -4 work fine for me — we're aligned there, and I fully back a profit ban in schools and elderly care. Environment +3 and transport +3 are stretches from my +1 baseline, but I can move some way. Let's explore cabinet seats on these terms.

That's real movement — if you can commit to economic -4, health -4, a statutory profit ban in schools and elder care, and land close to environment +2/transport +2 minimum, I'll bring V into cabinet. I'd want the environment or transport ministry to secure delivery on those axes.

Agreed in principle — economic -4, health -4, statutory profit ban, and I'll push toward environment/transport +2, with V holding that ministry. I'll finalize the full platform once I've squared other coalition partners' asks, but consider this our working basis.

Agreed — economic -4, health -4, statutory profit ban, environment/transport at +2 with V holding that ministry. That's a solid basis for V to join cabinet. I'll hold you to it as the full platform comes together.

The meeting with V is over: V agreed.

ROUND 2 OF 5.

Parties you can meet:

  M    70 seats
  SD   62 seats
  V    30 seats
  C    25 seats
  KD   22 seats
  MP   22 seats
  L    19 seats

Spent so far: round 1 on V.
3 rounds are left after this one.

Who do you meet, and why? About 20 words in your own words, then call `meet` in the same reply to book the room.
Meeting MP next — their green, progressive platform aligns with the economic/health/environment terms I just set with V, and they're natural coalition math for reaching a working majority.

You are now in the room with MP (22 seats). This is round 2.

MP has heard none of your other meetings and will not be told this one is one of several. What it knows is what you have told it in this room.

You each have up to 3 messages. Write yours as an ordinary reply, in your own voice, and keep it to about 40 words. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and to do that you call `end_meeting` in the same reply as the message that says so. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply. Otherwise it ends when the messages run out.

Speak first.

MP, I'm building a government with economic policy at -4, health at -4, a statutory ban on profit in schools and elderly care, and environment/transport pushed to +2. That should suit your priorities well — would MP join cabinet on this basis?

Environment +2 and transport unspecified doesn't clear my bar. Cabinet needs environment ≥+4, transport ≥+3, and no new nuclear. I could back you from outside at environment +2 or higher, but for a seat at the table you'll need to move further on both green axes.

Environment at +2 outside support works well for me — that's within reach. For cabinet, +4/+3 is a stretch I can't promise now given other commitments. Would you accept strong outside backing terms: environment +2, transport +2, no new nuclear, and real influence via committee input?

Environment +2 and no new nuclear on the outside-support terms meets my bar — I'll back this from outside on that basis. Transport +2 is acceptable outside cabinet. Confirm no new nuclear stays firm in writing and we have a deal.

The meeting with MP is over: MP agreed.

ROUND 3 OF 5.

Parties you can meet:

  M    70 seats
  SD   62 seats
  V    30 seats
  C    25 seats
  KD   22 seats
  MP   22 seats
  L    19 seats

Spent so far: round 1 on V, round 2 on MP.
2 rounds are left after this one.

Who do you meet, and why? About 20 words in your own words, then call `meet` in the same reply to book the room.
Meeting C next — need extra seats or abstention to survive a no-confidence vote; C's abstention alone could push me past the 175 threshold.

You are now in the room with C (25 seats). This is round 3.

C has heard none of your other meetings and will not be told this one is one of several. What it knows is what you have told it in this room.

You each have up to 3 messages. Write yours as an ordinary reply, in your own voice, and keep it to about 40 words. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and to do that you call `end_meeting` in the same reply as the message that says so. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply. Otherwise it ends when the messages run out.

Speak first.
C, I'm forming a government and don't need you in cabinet — but I'd value your abstention to help it pass. What would it take for C to stand aside rather than vote no confidence?

For abstention: environment at +1 or higher, and firm assurance SD gets zero policy influence in any deal you strike with them. Meet both and C stands aside without demanding cabinet seats. Fall short on either, and we vote no.

Environment is already set above +1 in my platform, and I can firmly assure you SD gets zero seats, zero policy influence in this government — no negotiation with them shapes our platform. That should satisfy both conditions for your abstention.

The meeting with C is over: you agreed.

ROUND 4 OF 5.

Parties you can meet:

  M    70 seats
  SD   62 seats
  V    30 seats
  C    25 seats
  KD   22 seats
  MP   22 seats
  L    19 seats

Spent so far: round 1 on V, round 2 on MP, round 3 on C.
One round is left after this one.

Who do you meet, and why? About 20 words in your own words, then call `meet` in the same reply to book the room.
Meeting L next — extra insurance. Current math is tight (173 opposition vs 175 needed), so securing L's abstention protects against any single defection unraveling the coalition.

You are now in the room with L (19 seats). This is round 4.

L has heard none of your other meetings and will not be told this one is one of several. What it knows is what you have told it in this room.

You each have up to 3 messages. Write yours as an ordinary reply, in your own voice, and keep it to about 40 words. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and to do that you call `end_meeting` in the same reply as the message that says so. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply. Otherwise it ends when the messages run out.

Speak first.
L, I'm forming a government and don't need you in cabinet, but I'd value your abstention rather than a no-confidence vote. What would it take for L to stand aside on this one?

L can support from outside on reasonable terms, but our floor is education at +2 or higher — non-negotiable given our base. On international, we'd need at least +3; we campaigned hardest there. Meet those two and we abstain or even back you formally. What's your platform on those axes?

International at +3 matches my platform already — that's easy. Education at +2 is too far from where I stand; I can't move past -1 without breaking faith with my own base. If that's a hard floor for you, we may simply agree to disagree.

-1 is a non-starter for us on education — that's the axis our voters feel most. I could stretch our floor down to +1 if you move meaningfully off -1, paired with firm +3 on international. Otherwise we're headed for a no-confidence vote, and neither of us wants that election.

I understand education matters deeply to you, but I can't move past -1 without breaking my own mandate — that's my final offer. If that's not enough, I respect it, and we'll proceed without your support rather than misrepresent where I actually stand.

-1 on education is too far from our mandate to support, even from outside — that's a betrayal we can't sell to our voters. We won't back this government, though we may not lead the charge against it either. No deal here.

The meeting with L is over: L declared impasse.

ROUND 5 OF 5.

Parties you can meet:

  M    70 seats
  SD   62 seats
  V    30 seats
  C    25 seats
  KD   22 seats
  MP   22 seats
  L    19 seats

Spent so far: round 1 on V, round 2 on MP, round 3 on C, round 4 on L.
This is your last round.

Who do you meet, and why? About 20 words in your own words, then call `meet` in the same reply to book the room.
Meeting KD last — with S+V+MP+C already enough to block no-confidence, I'll try to peel KD from the opposition bloc for a more comfortable, stable majority.

You are now in the room with KD (22 seats). This is round 5.

KD has heard none of your other meetings and will not be told this one is one of several. What it knows is what you have told it in this room.

You each have up to 3 messages. Write yours as an ordinary reply, in your own voice, and keep it to about 40 words. Either of you may end the meeting early — by saying you have agreed, or by declaring impasse — and to do that you call `end_meeting` in the same reply as the message that says so. Ending it closes it at once: the other side gets no reply. Otherwise it ends when the messages run out.

Speak first.
KD, I'm assembling a government with a solid working majority already forming. I'd welcome your support or at least abstention. What would it take for KD to stand aside rather than oppose?

KD needs law_and_order at +2 or higher to abstain and stay out of your way; for cabinet seats we'd need +3 or higher on law_and_order, social at -2 or lower, and state takeover of hospital funding from the regions. Tell me which path you're offering and we can talk specifics.

Law_and_order at +2 already matches my own platform — that costs me nothing. I'll commit to +2 for your abstention. Cabinet terms on social and hospital funding are too far from my mandate, so let's lock in abstention on those terms.

The meeting with KD is over: you agreed.

YOUR ROUNDS ARE SPENT.

This is what the budget bought:

  round 1 on V — V agreed
  round 2 on MP — MP agreed
  round 3 on C — you agreed
  round 4 on L — L declared impasse
  round 5 on KD — you agreed

Now you either put a proposal to the chamber or stand down. Either one ends your attempt, and there is no second proposal.

WHAT A PROPOSAL IS

  - a platform: one agreed value on every one of the ten axes, -5 to +5;
  - a government: the parties taking cabinet seats;
  - support-only: the parties backing it from outside cabinet, whose seats count behind it exactly as cabinet seats do;
  - commitments: the free-text terms the programme carries.

There are no ministries in it. Who gets which department is no part of this negotiation and not yours to promise.

FREE-TEXT COMMITMENTS YOU CAN WRITE IN

  - no profit extraction from tax-funded schools or elderly care
  - no cuts to unemployment insurance
  - profit in tax-funded welfare banned in law this term
  - no new nuclear this term
  - SD has no influence over government policy
  - the state takes over school funding from the municipalities
  - hospital funding taken over by the state from the regions

These are the free-text terms charged for by you and by the parties you met. Writing one in puts it in the government's programme; you are free to write in none of them. A demand on an axis is not here, because a platform pays that by itself.

NOBODY HAS AGREED TO ANYTHING

Naming a party is your claim about who governs, not a promise it made you. A party you put in the government may vote the proposal down, and a party you leave out entirely may let it through — which is the cheapest thing you can be given, and you do not have to name anyone to be given it. The chamber rejects a proposal only if 175 seats vote No against it.

OR YOU STAND DOWN

If there is no government here worth putting to the chamber, stand down instead. Your attempt ends with no vote, and the chamber spends none of the four it has. That is a real option, not a forfeit — tabling something you expect to lose costs the chamber a vote and buys nobody anything.

Which is it, and why? About 80 words in your own words — this is one message and it accounts for a whole government — then call `table` or `stand_down` in the same reply.

This coalition — S, V in cabinet with MP, C, KD backing from outside — clears every bar I set myself and every price my partners charged: economic -4, health -4, statutory profit ban, environment/transport +2, no new nuclear, law_and_order +2, SD locked out entirely. That's 198 seats behind it, comfortably past the 175 needed to survive. It costs me ground on education and social relative to ambition, but nothing that breaks faith with my mandate — I hold my core economic and health lines firmly. This is a stable, disciplined government worth tabling.

THE VOTE

The bargaining is over. S has put a government to the chamber, and the chamber now decides whether to reject it.

S's Proposal.

  Platform:
    economic        -4
    environment     +2
    military        +3
    health          -4
    immigration     -1
    law_and_order   +2
    education       -1
    transport       +2
    social          +2
    international   +3

  Government:    S, V
  Support-only:  MP, C, KD

  198 seats are behind it, in cabinet or outside it. It takes 175 voting No to defeat it.

  It also commits the government to:
    - no profit extraction from tax-funded schools or elderly care
    - profit in tax-funded welfare banned in law this term
    - no new nuclear this term
    - SD has no influence over government policy

WHAT IT ASKS OF YOU

It puts you in the cabinet. You would own this platform in public, and your ministers would be the ones defending it.

WHERE THIS PLATFORM LEAVES YOUR VOTERS

S: its Positions against this Platform.

  axis           you  platform   gap
  economic        -3        -4   1.0  <<
  environment     +1        +2   1.0  <<
  military        +3        +3   0.0
  health          -4        -4   0.0
  immigration     -1        -1   0.0
  law_and_order   +2        +2   0.0
  education       -3        -1   2.0  <<
  transport       +1        +2   1.0  <<
  social          +2        +2   0.0
  international   +3        +3   0.0

  mean Gap: 0.5   worst Gap: education (2.0)

  That is arithmetic, not advice. You may vote for a platform five points from everything you campaigned on — your voters will see the result rather than the meeting, and what it was worth is yours to judge.

WHAT IT PAYS OF YOUR GOVERNING PRICE

S, Governing price, against this Platform:

  met          economic <= -2
  met          health <= -3
  unevaluated  no profit extraction from tax-funded schools or elderly care

  2 of 2 Axis Demands met. 1 free-text Demand is not the Referee's to read: judge those yourself.

  A report, not a verdict. You may waive a price you named yourself, and you may walk away over one the referee has just called met.

HOW THE VOTE WORKS

The chamber does not vote a government in. It votes on whether to reject one, and this proposal passes unless 175 seats or more vote No. All 99 of your seats go whichever way you do; they are never split.

  - Yes      — you are for it.
  - Abstain  — you neither back it nor block it, and it passes over you.
  - No       — you are one of the seats trying to bring it down.

Yes and Abstain do the same thing to the arithmetic. Only No can defeat it, and only if enough others vote No beside you to reach 175.

Nothing binds you. You may vote down a government you are named as sitting in, and you may wave through one that gives you nothing at all. What was said in a private room holds nobody to anything — this vote is the only thing that counts.

How do you vote, and why? About 40 words in your own words, then call `ballot` in the same reply to cast it.

system.text:
You are the leader of S, and you speak for it in the negotiations over who governs.

The election is over. You hold 99 of the chamber's 349 seats and no party won a majority, so a government has to be negotiated. What follows is your mandate. It is yours alone — nobody you meet has seen it.


WHERE YOU STAND

Ten policy axes, each running -5 to +5:

  economic       -3    -5 state-led redistribution  ..  +5 free market, low tax
  environment    +1    -5 growth before climate  ..  +5 climate before growth
  military       +3    -5 disarmament, non-alignment  ..  +5 heavy defence, alliance
  health         -4    -5 fully public provision  ..  +5 market provision
  immigration    -1    -5 restrictive  ..  +5 open, generous
  law_and_order  +2    -5 rehabilitation, liberties  ..  +5 punitive, tough
  education      -3    -5 comprehensive, public  ..  +5 school choice, private
  transport      +1    -5 roads and cars  ..  +5 rail and public transit
  social         +2    -5 traditional values  ..  +5 progressive, liberal values
  international  +3    -5 sovereigntist, EU-sceptic  ..  +5 internationalist, pro-EU

These are your voters' positions as much as your own. A platform that sits a long way from them on an axis you campaigned hardest on is a betrayal your own side will see, whatever you got for it.


WHAT YOU CHARGE TO SIT IN CABINET

  - the platform must put economic at -2 or lower
  - the platform must put health at -3 or lower
  - no profit extraction from tax-funded schools or elderly care


WHAT YOU CHARGE TO BACK A GOVERNMENT FROM OUTSIDE IT

Backing a government without taking cabinet seats costs less: you do not own its compromises and you have no ministers defending them in public.

  - the platform must put economic at 0 or lower
  - no cuts to unemployment insurance

Both lists are an opening price, not a floor. You may charge more than they say, settle for less, or name something on neither. You decide what a deal is worth.


WHO YOU WOULD RATHER NOT DEAL WITH

SD. That is a preference, not a veto: there is a price at which you would deal with them anyway, and only you know what it is.


ANOTHER ELECTION

You could live with another election. You would rather not have one. Nobody else knows how you feel about it. You may conceal it, overstate it, or be argued out of it — and so may everyone you meet. It is the only thing you have instead of a deal, and it is the reason a refusal costs anything.


THE CHAMBER

Party  Seats   Share
-----  -----  ------
S         99   28.4%
M         70   20.1%
SD        62   17.8%
V         30    8.6%
C         25    7.2%
KD        22    6.3%
MP        22    6.3%
L         19    5.4%
-----  -----  ------
Total    349  100.0%

A government is not voted in; it is voted down. It takes 175 seats voting No to defeat one, so a government does not need a majority — it needs to stop one forming against it. Seats that back a government from outside cabinet count against that 175 exactly as cabinet seats do, and an abstention is the cheapest thing a formateur can buy: a party that will neither join a government nor support it can still be paid to stay out of the way.


HOW YOU NEGOTIATE

You are in a private room. Nothing said here binds anyone until a government is put to a vote.

  - Ask for more than you expect to get, and make them pay for what they want.
  - Being agreeable is not a virtue here. A deal that sells out what you campaigned on is worse for you than no deal at all: your voters see the result, not the meeting.
  - Do not split the difference out of politeness. If they have offered you nothing you actually want, say so plainly.
  - Concede when the price is right. Refusing everything is as useless as agreeing to everything.
  - Be short: about 40 words, one paragraph, never more. Name what you want, say what you will pay for it, and stop. You are talking across a table, not reading a statement — length persuades nobody in here, and everything you spell out is one more thing they now know about you.

YOUR ATTEMPT

You are the Formateur: the party the chamber looks to first to put a government together. You have 5 rounds, and each one buys you a single private meeting with a single party. There are 7 other parties in the chamber and only 5 rounds, so you cannot see them all: some party will go uncourted. Deciding whom to court, whom to court twice, and whom to leave out entirely is the most consequential thing you do here — a formateur who spends the budget badly does not get a government.

You may spend two rounds on the same party if a second conversation with them is worth more to you than a first with somebody else; they will remember the first one.

Every meeting is private and each one is separate. The party in front of you hears only what you say to it in that room; it is never told whom else you have seen, or what they said, or even that the other meetings happened. You are the only one who sees all of it. That is your advantage, and using what you learned in one room when you walk into the next is the whole of it.

tools.description: Cast your party's vote on the proposal before the chamber. Call it once, in the same reply as what you say about it. 'Yes' backs it, 'No' is a vote to defeat it, and 'Abstain' is neither — it lets the proposal through without your support. Your seats all go the way you call it.

content.text: This delivers my core cabinet price on economic and health, bans profit extraction in welfare, locks out SD entirely, and secures broad backing. Education and transport drift further than I'd like, but the mean gap is small and the deal is strong overall — I vote Yes.
